mcq.question: When is returning an error value (such as a Result or std::error_code) a better choice than throwing an exception?

options.A: Never – exceptions are always better in C++
options.C: When failure is an ordinary, expected outcome that the immediate caller will handle, such as a mistyped seat code
options.D: When the error must cross many layers of the call stack

mcq.explanation: Exceptions suit rare failures the immediate caller cannot fix. Expected failures are part of normal control flow, and an explicit return value makes handling them visible and cheap.

mcq.question: What does specialising `std::is_error_code_enum<seat_errc>` enable?

options.B: Implicit conversion of `seat_errc` values to `std::error_code`, using the `make_error_code` found by argument-dependent lookup

mcq.explanation: With the trait set, `std::error_code ec = seat_errc::empty;` calls your `make_error_code`, which attaches your custom category.

bonus.question: A deep exception hierarchy can mirror every possible failure. How deep should it be, and how do you decide which failures deserve their own class?
Write a failing test for a `try_book` function that returns `Result<std::string>` instead of throwing for a taken seat, then implement it on top of `BoxOffice`.
